 8 dengue deaths recorded in Iloilo City
 By Rjay Zuriaga Castor
 November 9, 2026
 10
 Resize 
 Small 
 Medium 
 Large 
 LOILO CITY — Dengue infections here have climbed by 37.7 percent this year, with eight deaths recorded as of Oct. 31, prompting health authorities to step up mosquito control operations and call for earlier medical intervention.
 City Health Office (CHO) head Dr. Mary Ann Diaz said the city logged 785 dengue cases from Jan. 4 to Oct.
 31, surpassing the number recorded during the same period last year.
 She confirmed that the city had already breached both the alert and epidemic thresholds for dengue infections.
 Of the eight fatalities, one case recorded in February involved a 14-year-old boy from Baldoza, La Paz.

 Four more deaths occurred in August: a seven-year-old girl from Lopez Jaena Norte; a four-year-old boy from Dela Rama; a 49-year-old woman from Filomena, Arevalo; and an eight-year-old child from Mansaya, Lapuz.
 The remaining three fatalities were recorded in September involving a 32-year-old woman from Boulevard, Molo; a 12-year-old girl from San Isidro, Jaro; and an eight-year-old girl from Baldoza, La Paz.
 Advertisement 
 The CHO also identified dengue clusters in 28 villages, four of which were classified as hotspots.
 Hinactacan recorded the highest number of clustered cases at 10, followed by San Isidro in Jaro with eight and Tabuc Suba in Jaro with seven.
 MV Hechanova and Dela Rama each logged six clustered cases, while So-oc, Dulunan and Burgos-Mabini recorded five each.
 Diaz said surveillance data showed that areas with more infections and fatalities were generally densely populated communities where garbage accumulation and stagnant water provided potential mosquito breeding grounds.
 Advertisement 
 She said the CHO was intensifying its prevention campaign under the 4S strategy, particularly the search and destruction of mosquito breeding sites and the promotion of early consultation.
 Diaz urged households to conduct daily clean-up activities rather than depend solely on scheduled weekly barangay clean-ups.
 “If there are no mosquito breeding sites, there will be no mosquitoes and, consequently, no dengue cases. This is why we are campaigning for massive and intensive cleanup activities in barangays,” she said.
 She reminded that patients should seek medical attention as soon as they develop a fever, citing cases in which fatalities were brought to health facilities only after their conditions had deteriorated.
 Advertisement 
 Residents can avail themselves of free consultations and dengue testing at any of the city’s nine district health centers, which are equipped with Dengue NS1 testing kits.
 Diaz cautioned that dengue may initially present only as fever, including lowgrade fever, without other immediately noticeable symptoms.
 She warned against waiting for bleeding manifestations, such as nosebleeds, bleeding gums or vomiting blood, before consulting a doctor, as these may signal severe disease or complications.
 Meanwhile, the city’s sanitation division has completed its second round of routine misting operations across all 180 villages, with communities reporting dengue infections prioritized, followed by neighboring areas.
 Advertisement 
 The CHO is also conducting intensive clean-up activities ahead of misting operations, prioritizing the eight villages where dengue-related deaths have been recorded.
 Barangay Dengue Task Forces and Barangay Health Emergency Response Teams have likewise been activated to identify residents with fever, encourage prompt consultation and monitor reported infections.
